Personal minimums (editable) BALLOON

Saved separately per aircraft on this device — Balloon and Airplane each keep their own numbers. Switch MODE (top) and the fields swap to that aircraft's set. Crosswind max lives in the Airplane panel.
  • Balloon: the surface, 500–1500 transport and sfc→500 shear limits gate the launch & low-level window.
  • Balloon clouds: the min ceiling is measured against the lowest cloud of any layer (FEW+), not just BKN/OVC — a balloon can't dodge cloud — with a 500 ft below-cloud buffer surfaced as CAUTION (the §91.155 Class E figure; in Class G at or below 1,200 ft AGL by day the rule is clear of clouds + 1 SM — treat 500 ft as a personal margin). (Airplane mode keeps the BKN/OVC ceiling.)
  • Airplane / XC: set your crosswind limit in the Airplane panel (beside the runways); freezing level & icing layers are flagged in the briefing.
  • Ceiling, visibility, gust and density-altitude minimums apply in every mode.

    Flyability — is it flyable, and when

    Fetch winds aloft for the 24-hour flyability ribbon.
    Each row graded per hour vs your personal minimums — green within limits, amber within ~30%, red busts. VERDICT = worst row that hour. NOW marked; times Zulu. DAY / NIGHT row uses the 14 CFR 1.1 clock: blue = day, violet = civil twilight (still legal day, but position lights are required after sunset), slate = night. CROSSWIND row appears in airplane mode when a runway is set — the component on the best (into-wind) runway vs your crosswind max.
    DAWN & DUSK WINDOWS BALLOON
    Fetch winds aloft to score your flight windows.
    Two windows a day — the calm just after sunrise and the ~2 h before sunset. Every forecast hour is scored against your personal minimums; the bracketed bands are the flyable windows, each with its own worst-case verdict. Window edges: sunrise −15→+90 min, sunset −120→0 min (operational, not regulatory). Sun times in UTC (Zulu).
    FLYABLE WINDOWS AIRPLANE · CONDITIONS-BASED
    Fetch winds aloft to score your flight windows.
    Unlike the balloon dawn/dusk bands, these are conditions-based — every forecast hour is scored against your personal minimums and the contiguous flyable stretches (any time of day) are bracketed, each with its worst-case verdict. Times Zulu.

    Balloon Tether — 0–250 ft assessment

    Fetch winds aloft for the tether assessment.
    Grades the worst wind from the surface to your tether ceiling (10 m & 80 m AGL bracket 0–250 ft), with a surface→top shear-trap flag and a convective veto (tethered balloons must come down for any convection). Model boundary-layer winds are smoothed — a stable evening can hide low-level shear, so cross-check surface obs. Tethers usually run ~4–11 pm local; other hours flagged. Times Zulu.

    7-Day Tether Outlook

    Fetch a forecast for the 7-day tether outlook.
    Plan an event days out: each day’s best evening (4–11 pm ET) tether window vs your limits, with an improving/degrading trend. Uses the ceiling/steady/gust limits from the Balloon Tether panel. Times Zulu.

    Heat-Burst Watch

    Fetch a forecast to assess heat-burst potential.
    A heat burst is a collapsing-storm downdraft punching through a deep, dry sub-cloud layer: rain evaporates, the air warms dry-adiabatically on the way down, and the surface sees a sudden temperature spike, a dewpoint crash, and strong dry gusts (often at night). The chart plots temperature, dewpoint and gusts so the signature is visible at a glance. Times Zulu.

    Flight category & VFR → IMC watch

    VFR → IMC watch

    Fetch winds aloft for the VFR-into-IMC deterioration watch.
    • Continued VFR into IMC is the leading cause of fatal GA weather accidents — a non-instrument pilot can lose control within minutes of entering cloud.
    • The trap is gradual: scattered → broken → overcast, visibility slowly dropping, plus "get-there-itis." This strip makes the trend explicit.
    • Defense: hard personal minimums, a turn-back / divert time decided before takeoff, and a no-go if conditions are trending toward your minimums inside the window.
    • Categories use model ceiling + visibility (a proxy) — cross-check TAFs and PIREPs.

    Forecast confidence (ensemble)BALLOON

    loads with the forecast
    Ensemble confidence loads with the forecast.
    • What this is: a second live call to Open-Meteo’s GFS ensemble (31 perturbed members). Where the members agree, the forecast is confident; where they scatter, it isn’t.
    • The headline reads how many members keep surface wind & gust inside your personal minimums at the target hour — a probabilistic GO/NO-GO around the single-forecast verdict above.
    • Wide spread / split members = the atmosphere is hard to pin down right now; treat a GO as marginal and recheck nearer launch. This panel never overrides the verdict — it tells you how much to trust it.

    Model consensusBALLOON

    loads with the forecast
    Model consensus loads with the forecast.
    • What this is: a third live call asking up to nine independent global models — GFS (NOAA), ECMWF (EU), ICON (DWD), GEM (Canada), ARPEGE (France), UKMO, JMA, CMA & ACCESS — for the surface wind & gust at your target hour; any with no data for your point drop out.
    • TL;DR: how many models keep wind & gust inside your personal minimums. All agreeing = high confidence; a split means the models genuinely disagree on your launch hour. Collapsed, the header shows the tally + a per-model colour strip (green ok · amber marginal · red over).
    • This is cross-model agreement (different physics), complementing the ensemble above (one model, many perturbed members). It never overrides the verdict; on any outage it shows “unavailable.”

    Active alerts & warnings (NWS)

    Active watches, warnings & advisories load with the forecast.
    • What this is: live NWS active alerts for your exact lat/lon (CAP feed). An active Tornado or Severe Thunderstorm Warning (or any Severe/Extreme warning) forces the verdict to NO-GO; a Watch or advisory softens it to CAUTION.
    • Like the discussion, it can tighten the verdict but never loosens one — it never creates a GO and never clears a NO-GO. On any outage or outside US coverage it shows “unavailable” and changes nothing.
    • Alerts cover a county/zone polygon; the onset/end times and the headline tell you whether it overlaps your launch window. You remain PIC.

    Forecaster discussion (AFD)

    Forecaster discussion loads with the forecast.
    • What this is: the live NWS Area Forecast Discussion for your launch office (resolved from your lat/lon) — the human forecaster’s reasoning on timing, convection & hazards that the wind panels and radar do not model.
    • Hazard scan flags convective / wind-shear / IFR mentions and shows the sentence so you judge timing & area; a convective mention can soften a wind-GO to CAUTION, but never overrides a NO-GO and never turns a NO-GO into GO.
    • The AFD covers the whole forecast area; boundaries it names (“north of I-70”) may or may not include your point. Read it — you remain PIC.

    Best windows (ensemble)BALLOON

    Best windows load with the ensemble forecast.
    • Scans the next ~48 h of the GFS ensemble and ranks the stretches where most members keep surface wind & gust inside your minimums — a planning view on top of the confidence panel.
    • Each window shows mean member agreement (your confidence it stays flyable), length, day/night, and the median surface-wind range. The ★ marks the top pick.
    • Hour resolution, model winds only — it finds candidate windows; always confirm the launch-time forecast, daylight/currency rules and official products before committing.

    Clouds, layers & fog

    Fetch winds aloft to read cloud layers and fog risk.
    • Coverage: FEW / SCT / BKN / OVC ≈ 1–2 / 3–4 / 5–7 / 8 eighths of sky. A ceiling is the lowest BKN/OVC layer, or the vertical visibility (VV) into an obscuration (14 CFR 1.1). In balloon mode the verdict counts the lowest cloud of any layer (FEW+) — a balloon can't sidestep cloud.
    • Radiation fog forms on clear, calm, moist nights as the surface cools to the dewpoint — watch a small dewpoint depression (T−Td) collapsing toward dawn with light wind. It's a VFR no-go until it burns off.
    • Layers are derived from model cloud cover at pressure levels — a proxy for layer bases, not a pilot report.

    Surface watch-board — past + forecast

    Fetch winds aloft to load the watch-board (past + forecast 10 m wind & gusts).
    Upwind now — neighbour stations
    Fetch to compare the launch against upwind/downwind neighbours.
    Model surface winds at each point (Open-Meteo) — not METARs (those are CORS-blocked from a static file). Upwind / cross / downwind is judged against the launch surface-wind direction; the arrival estimate is naive straight-line advection (distance ÷ launch surface speed) and assumes the pattern simply translates — real boundaries strengthen, decay, and turn.

    Daylight & twilight — window boundaries

    Set lat/lon/date — civil dawn, sunrise, sunset & civil dusk compute in UTC (Zulu), no network.
    • There is no FAA night rating; three different clocks apply. Sunset → sunrise: position lights must be lit (14 CFR 91.209(a)); anticollision lights whenever installed, day or night (91.209(b)); Special VFR also keys on sunset/sunrise (91.157(e)). Civil dusk → civil dawn (“night”, 1.1): night logging, the 91.155 night minimums, and the 61.109/61.129 night-training hours. Sunset + 1 h → sunrise − 1 h: to carry passengers you need 3 takeoffs & landings to a full stop in the prior 90 days flown in that window, as sole manipulator, in the same category and class — balloon landings don’t count for the Archer and vice versa (61.57(b)). The clocks table below gives tonight’s times.
    • FAA “night” for logging & most Part 91 night rules (14 CFR 1.1) = end of evening civil twilight → beginning of morning civil twilight — i.e. the civil dusk → civil dawn times above (sun’s center 6° below the horizon, per the Air Almanac).
    • Civil dawn is the earliest usable light; civil dusk is the hard outside edge for recovery light. Sunrise/sunset here is the sun’s upper limb on the horizon (refraction included).
    • The flyable windows bracketed in the Flyability windows above are an operational heuristic — morning ≈ sunrise −15 → +90 min, evening ≈ sunset −120 → 0 — not regulatory. The 15 min before sunrise is still “sunset → sunrise” for 91.209(a): position lights lit until sunrise.

    Wind heatmap — altitude × time

    Fetch winds aloft to build the altitude × time wind grid.
    • Each square = wind at that altitude (500 ft steps to 4,000 ft AGL) for that hour, next 24 h. X-axis is local clock hour (00–23), not hours-from-now.
    • Green / amber / red = speed banded at your transport limit (≤ limit−2 / near / over).
    • Arrows point the way the air drifts (where it carries you). Hover a square for the wind in METAR form — DIR@SPEED, the direction it's from (e.g. 250@18KT).
    • Cyan outline = ≥7 kt vector shear from the layer below — a shear zone.
    • ◆ = a wind-speed maximum aloft (possible nocturnal low-level jet).
    • Cyan outline = shear zone: the wind vector changes sharply across 500 ft (speed, direction, or both).
    • The dangerous combo: strong speed shear + a directional veer in the same layer = classic low-level wind shear — hazardous on climb-out/approach, a basket-spinner for balloons.
    • ◆ = wind max aloft: often a nocturnal low-level jet — the surface decouples overnight and a fast ribbon forms a few hundred to ~2,000 ft up.
    • Takeaway: a dawn balloon can be glassy at the ground yet ripping a few hundred feet above — read the whole column, not just the surface.

    Drift — 3D · map · plan · fronts cube

    Fetch winds aloft, then load the drift map.
    Ground sites:
    • Plots your projected drift track on a topographic base (Esri World Topo), launch (green) to landing (red), with 15-min time ticks and a 1 NM scale bar.
    • Same single-forecast drift as the plan view, now geographically placed so you can eyeball roads, water, towns and open fields under the path. The dashed magenta cone (amber dots) shows where the ensemble’s surface-wind disagreement would scatter your landing — load the map after winds finish fetching.
    • Topo tiles are for orientation only — not a substitute for a current sectional or obstacle data. Loads tiles from Esri when you press the button.
    Integrates the profile winds along your vertical schedule (1-min steps): climb → hold ceiling → step down through the mid band → ride near surface to the end. N-up, launch at the cross, rings in NM, colour = altitude. Estimate only — real drift varies with the actual column and with timing through the evening.
    3D cube — local wind & synoptic fronts
    Rotatable model wind volume around your site at the target time. Separate fetch (5×5 grid × 7 levels). Top alt, arrow density & size adjust below — redraw only, no re-fetch.
    Reuses the synoptic surface grid (loads it if needed). Red = warm air advecting in, blue = cold — the two masses meet at the front.
    Multi-level Soft voxel stack — pick a footprint, then Load. 24 h window at 3 h steps. Throttled.
    Load to build the cube. It reuses the synoptic grid (~990 mi), tilts the warm/cold-advection field into a translucent volume, and lets you bias the view toward one air mass.
    • Each arrow is the model wind at a grid point and altitude, pointing the way the air drifts; color runs low → high (surface → ~18,000 ft). A single-site volume centred on your Airport/GPS point — not the flight path (that's the drift track above). N/E/S/W label the floor; heights label the axis. Tick Follow flight path to size the box to your projected drift and thread the magenta track through it (white dot = launch, amber = end); the zoom slider scales the whole volume uniformly — the path widens and climbs together, not just vertically. Drag to rotate.
    • In flight: arrows that fan out or twist with height (veer / backing) = shear — expect a bumpier ride and your drift direction shifting as you climb; tightly aligned arrows = a smooth, predictable column. Colour = altitude (surface → ~18,000 ft), so you can spot the level where the wind changes. Horizontal footprint is ~±25 NM — your actual local field.
    • Vertical axis uses standard-atmosphere heights for the pressure levels (10 m, 925, 850, 700, 500 hPa); horizontal spread is ~±25 NM around your site.
    • A target-time snapshot and a model-derived proxy — it shows structure (veer, shear, convergence), not a substitute for a sounding. Time animation is queued.
    • Red columns = warm advection (warm air moving in, ahead of a warm front); blue = cold advection (behind a cold front). Column height & opacity track advection strength — the back axis reads it in °C/h, and the floor label gives the column footprint & total span. Drag the cube to rotate.
    • In flight: a tall red column = warm air arriving there — destabilizing, usually ahead of a warm front (building cloud, rising wind); a tall blue column = cold air arriving — post-frontal gusts, drying, clearing but bumpy. Read the masses against your launch at centre to see what’s moving toward you. Each column covers ~100 NM of ground; the whole field spans ~860 NM, so this is the big picture, not your local field.
    • Bias fades one mass so you can see the other through it; Extent zooms from a tight local view out to the full ~990 mi grid.
    • Surface-only for now (one tilted layer); a true multi-level vertical stack is the planned upgrade. Model-derived proxy, valid ~now.

    Terrain under driftBALLOON

    Fetch winds aloft, then load the terrain profile.
    • Samples Open-Meteo’s Copernicus 90 m elevation at up to 80 points along your projected drift track and draws the ground beneath your planned altitude — both in ft MSL.
    • Because the balloon climbs above launch elevation, rising terrain downwind eats into your clearance even at a fixed altitude. The dashed line marks the minimum-clearance point.
    • Bare-earth model — no towers, antennas or trees. Always confirm obstacles and landing options on a current sectional.

    Profile plot

    Y = altitude (ft AGL) · X = wind speed (kt). Amber dashed line = transport (500–1500 ft) limit · green band (left) = surface comfort speeds. Dots/line: green within limit · amber within 2 kt · red over (surface vs your surface min, aloft vs transport).

    Wind profile — table

    Auto-fills from Open-Meteo on fetch (marked OM). Open-Meteo low-level is a coarse blend — overwrite 500–1500 ft from your pibal or a RAP/HRRR sounding (those are the deciders). Any edit recomputes the verdict.
    Tierktfrom°→ tosrc
    from° is the standard (METAR / winds-aloft) convention — the direction the wind comes from. → to is the reciprocal: the way a balloon actually drifts; the arrow is drawn north-up.

    Severe kinematics — shear, helicity & storm mode

    Fetch winds aloft for shear & helicity.
    Bulk shear = vector wind change across a layer; SRH = storm-relative helicity (low-level rotation potential), for the Bunkers right-moving storm. Model-derived & smoothed — planning-grade situational awareness, not a tornado forecast; the radiosonde panel is your observed ground truth. 0–6 km shear, storm motion & SRH use the 500 hPa deep layer (auto-fetched with the forecast).

    Hodograph — wind by altitude

    Dots = drift direction & speed (kt rings) at each altitude, surface→2000 ft. Tight cluster = uniform column, can't steer with altitude; a fan = altitude changes your drift (pick an altitude to steer).Tight cluster = little directional shear; a fan = wind veers with height — expect changing crosswind & drift through the climb/descent. Hover a dot — or read the keyed list — for altitude: dir° @ speed. Updates with the table.

    Steering solution finderBALLOON

    Fetch winds aloft to find a steering solution.
    • How it works: a balloon goes where the wind at its altitude pushes it — drift is the reciprocal of the wind direction. This reads the surface–2000 ft wind column (the hodograph) backwards: you name a heading, it finds the altitude that drifts that way.
    • The “box”: when one altitude drifts one way and another drifts back, you can launch, change altitude between them, and return near your launch point — the classic Albuquerque box. The finder flags it when the column supports it.
    • Resolution is the six profile tiers (surface, 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 ft). Treat a match as “around this altitude,” and confirm with a pibal or tissue-paper check before committing.

    Cross-discipline metrics (Open-Meteo)

    Fetch winds aloft to compute gust factor, cloud base, steerability & pressure trend.
    Adapted from soaring / paraglider / ballooning practice: gust factor (PG roughness), cloud base (LCL) (soaring Cu base / fog tell), steerability (surface-vs-3k direction split — the Albuquerque “box”)wind veer (surface-vs-3k direction change with height), and 3-h pressure tendency (frontal/gust precursor). All derived from data already on hand.

    Inversion lid & break timing

    Fetch winds aloft to analyse the temperature profile and inversion lid.
    • Temperature vs height from Open-Meteo pressure levels. A morning radiation inversion (cold at the surface, a warm "nose" aloft) caps a smooth surface layer.
    • The lid breaks when the daytime mixed layer climbs through the inversion top and winds aloft start mixing down. Break time is estimated from the forecast mixing-height series crossing the lid.
    • Resolution caveat: the model gives the surface plus pressure levels, so a shallow inversion's top snaps to the lowest level (often a few hundred ft). Read it as "a shallow surface inversion exists," not an exact lid height.
    • What it is: overnight the ground radiates heat to space and chills the air touching it — coldest at the surface, warmer just above (opposite of the normal lapse).
    • Why dawn is glassy: that stable cap decouples the surface from the wind aloft.
    • The break: after sunrise a mixed layer grows from the ground; when it climbs past the lid, faster air mixes down and the calm ends.
    • Two criteria together: surface inversion present + mixing height below its top → smooth surface likely holds; mixing height above the lid → roughening.
    • Marginal case: a sub-2 °C inversion already mixed out (mixing height ≫ lid) is noise-level, not a flight factor.

    Airplane — wind components, freezing level, cruise winds

    Fetch winds aloft to compute crosswind components, freezing level, and cruise winds.
    • Components: headwind = wind × cos(angle to runway), crosswind = wind × sin(angle). Pick the end with a headwind; check the crosswind against your personal max.
    • True vs magnetic: model winds are referenced to true north, runways are magnetic. The Mag var field converts (≈ 4°W in Indiana) — "west is best, add."
    • Freezing level is the floor of potential structural icing: in visible moisture at/above it you can pick up ice; the above-freezing layer below is the out.
    • Ceiling, visibility, gust, and density-altitude minimums in Settings apply to airplane mode too.

    Icing — structural & carburetor

    Fetch winds aloft to assess icing.
    • Structural icing needs supercooled liquid water — visible moisture (cloud) at 0 to about −20 °C, worst −2 to −15 °C. Your out is a layer that's above-freezing or clear of cloud (climb or descend).
    • Carburetor icing can form even on warm, humid days: a carb's venturi + fuel vaporization drops induction-air temperature ~20–30 °C, so serious icing happens at temps well above freezing. Apply carb heat per your POH.
    • Fuel-injected engines (e.g. the IO-370) aren't carb-ice-prone, though impact/induction icing can still occur in heavy moisture.
    • These are chart/model approximations, not an official icing forecast (G-AIRMET Zulu / FIP) — cross-check before flight.

    Route — multi-leg (airports)

    Enter 2+ airport IDs (departure first). Each waypoint is checked at its ETA — flight category, ceiling/vis, IFR alternate (1-2-3), and a night-arrival flag. Tick refuel at a stop to reset the elapsed clock.
    • ETE/ETA use your departure-site winds aloft + cruise TAS applied to every leg (a planning approximation), with the target hour as departure time.
    • Each waypoint is a snapshot at its ETA, not a continuous en-route forecast. Max 8 legs — split longer trips.
    • The 1-2-3 flag reflects forecast ceiling/vis only. A destination with no published instrument approach requires an alternate regardless of the forecast.
    • Waypoint ceilings use model pressure-level cloud (≥50%); a low surface deck can be under-detected — cross-check METAR/TAF.
    • Per-leg max terrain is sampled from the Copernicus surface DEM (90 m). MSA* ≈ terrain + 1,000 ft. The single-engine service ceiling (default Seminole PA-44-180 ≈ 3,800 ft — verify your POH) is degraded by departure density altitude, then compared per leg — multi-engine only: for a single-engine aircraft an engine failure is a glide, not a drift-down to a service ceiling, so this check doesn’t apply.
    • *MSA here is a centerline estimate (max terrain along the leg + 1,000 ft), not a charted MSA/MEA: no ±4 NM corridor and no charted obstacles — cross-check charts.

    Direct-to / HSI

    Optional. Enter a destination lat/lon to see course/distance/ETE. There's no "From" field — it's automatic: your live GPS fix while a track runs, otherwise the launch point.
    • Destination/airplane-oriented. In a balloon you usually don't have a fixed landing point, so this is optional — leave it blank and it stays idle.
    • The green pointer = course to the destination you enter; the white dashed = your current drift track. If they diverge, a different steering layer is needed.
    • "From" is automatic (live GPS while tracking, else launch) — there's no field to fill. ETE assumes the present drift holds.
    • Destination ceiling comes from model cloud cover at pressure levels (lowest layer ≥50% cloud — slightly conservative vs the broken ≥5/8 convention) and can under-detect a low surface deck/fog below ~360 ft AGL — cross-check the METAR/TAF.
    • A balloon-native version is queued for the airplane/mode split.
    • Instead of "navigate to a point" (no yoke to do it), it'll answer "given my drift, what fields/roads are in my landing footprint?" — the reverse of direct-to.

    Turbulence profile (surface → 6,000 ft)

    Fetch winds aloft to build the turbulence profile.
    • How it’s built: vertical wind shear between levels (10 m, 80 m and the 1000–700 hPa winds aloft) gives mechanical/clear-air turbulence in kt per 1000 ft (FAA Aviation Weather Handbook: ≥6 kt/1000 ft is the threshold for probable moderate-or-greater turbulence); CAPE + boundary-layer height give daytime thermal bumps below the convective top; the surface gust factor gives low-level mechanical roughness.
    • Colors: smooth · light · moderate · strong. The dashed blue line is the estimated convective top (thermals live below it in daytime).
    • Altitudes are ft MSL (winds-aloft / PIREP convention); the bold line is field elevation. This is a model estimate — confirm with G-AIRMET Tango, Graphical Turbulence Guidance and PIREPs before you launch.

    Ride quality — low-level turbulence

    Fetch winds aloft to estimate ride quality.
    • Mechanical turbulence comes from wind and gusts (worse over rough terrain); shear from fast changes of wind with height (the heatmap's cyan zones); thermal from daytime heating — a steep low-level lapse and CAPE mean convective bumps.
    • For a balloon the target is smooth; for a glider those thermal bumps are lift; for an airplane it's ride comfort and workload.
    • A boundary-layer proxy from wind, shear, lapse and CAPE — not a turbulence (G-AIRMET Tango / EDR) forecast.

    Density altitude — performance

    Fetch winds aloft for density-altitude performance.
    • Density altitude is the altitude your aircraft "feels" — it climbs with heat, humidity, and field elevation. High / hot / heavy is the classic departure-accident setup.
    • Airplane: longer takeoff roll and anemic climb. Balloon: thinner air gives less envelope lift, so reduced payload or more burner — worst on hot afternoons.
    • The percentages are generic light-piston rules of thumb — use your POH performance charts or the Koch chart for real numbers.

    Thermals & soaring

    Fetch winds aloft for the thermal / soaring forecast.
    • Parcel method: lift a surface parcel up the dry adiabat (3 °C/1000 ft). Where it stays warmer than the environment it's buoyant — a thermal. The thermal top is where parcel and environment temperatures meet.
    • Trigger temperature is the surface temp needed before thermals break through; once the day heats to it, expect convection to the thermal top.
    • Cumulus form if the condensation level is below the thermal top; otherwise "blue" thermals (no cloud markers — harder to read).
    • Model-profile proxy — refine with a soaring forecast (RASP / Dr Jack) and your own read of the sky.

    Synoptic map — pressure, highs/lows, frontal zones

    ~990 mi across (≈860 NM) around your site, valid now, derived from the Open-Meteo surface grid.
    Click "Load synoptic map" to fetch the regional grid and draw isobars, highs/lows, and frontal zones. Works from the downloaded file (Open-Meteo is CORS-open).
    • Thin lines = isobars (MSL pressure, 4 hPa apart). Tightly packed = strong pressure gradient = stronger wind.
    • H / L = surface high / low centers (with central hPa). Wind circles clockwise/out of a High, counter-clockwise/into a Low (N. hemisphere).
    • Shaded bands = thermal-gradient (frontal) zones: blue where cold air is advecting in (cold-front side), red where warm air is advecting (warm-front side). Opacity tracks gradient strength.
    • Drawn frontal lines follow the gradient ridge: a blue line with triangles = cold front, a red line with bumps = warm front. Glyphs point the way the front is moving. Model-derived proxy — not the official WPC analysis.
    • ◎ = your launch site. This is a model-derived proxy, not the official analysis — cross-check the WPC surface analysis.
    • Why it matters: the synoptic pattern sets your whole day — a passing front flips wind direction, spikes gust and shear, and drops ceilings; an approaching Low means deteriorating conditions.
    • Reading advection: the tint is computed as −(wind · temperature-gradient). Wind carrying cold air toward warm = cold advection (behind a cold front); the reverse = warm advection (ahead of a warm front).
    • Limits: drawn from a coarse surface grid, valid roughly now; it shows zones and tendency, not exact frontal lines. Frontal-line drawing + passage timing come next.

    Flight debrief — track vs forecast

    Import a KML (gx:Track) or GPX file from your flight logger. The track stays in this page only.

    Launch window scorer — best 30-min slot

    Fetch winds aloft to score launch slots.

    Precip radar (RainViewer composite)

    Click "Load / refresh radar" for the latest RainViewer precipitation composite (animated loop) over a topo base, centered on your lat/lon. White ring = launch.
    RainViewer composite loop on an Esri topo base — past ~2 h at 10-min steps plus a nowcast frame, zoom capped at 7 (RainViewer's max) so the layers align. Tiles + timeline load from the network (works in the downloaded file; the in-chat preview may block them). Cross-read with dewpoint depression: echoes into very dry air can fall as virga and kick out gusty outflow.

    Radiosonde ground-truth (U. Wyoming)

    Real weather-balloon (radiosonde) ascents at 00Z/12Z — the ground-truth the model is trying to reproduce. Cross-check the app's profile and inversion lid against the sounding: compare low-level DRCT/SKNT (wind) tier by tier, and look for TEMP rising with height (the inversion). Links open the U. Wyoming page (network; works anywhere a browser can reach the site). Upwind site = the air headed your way.

    Sources & methods

    Every computed value below is traceable to an authoritative source. This is a planning aid — see the disclaimer at the end.
    • Flight category (LIFR <500 ft/<1 SM · IFR 500–<1000/1–<3 · MVFR 1000–3000/3–5 · VFR >3000/>5) — Aviation Weather Handbook, FAA-H-8083-28B §3.4.2.14. These are situational-awareness categories, not the 14 CFR §91.155 VFR minimums.
    • Pressure altitude — ICAO Standard Atmosphere barometric relation. Density altitude — exact dry-air density relation DA = 145442.16·(1−(ρ/ρ₀)0.234969) from station pressure & OAT; defined in FAA-H-8083-28B §8.4.1.5 (worked example PA 10,000 ft @ 20°C → ~12,700 ft; this tool computes ~12,790 ft).
    • Cloud base (LCL) — Espy’s equation, ≈410 ft per °C of dewpoint spread (T−Td).
    • CAPE (J/kg; >0 unstable, thunderstorm environments often >1,000, extreme >5,000) — FAA-H-8083-28B Ch.13, Atmospheric Stability.
    • Ventilation rate (k kt·ft) = transport wind (vector-mean wind through the mixed layer) × mixing height; dispersion bands poor <40 / fair 40–60 / good 60–100 / very good 100–150 / excellent ≥150 — USDA Ag Handbook 360 “Fire Weather” (ventilation & transport wind); NWS fire-weather smoke-dispersal categories.
    • Gust / gust factor — a gust is a wind-speed fluctuation of ≥10 kt between peaks and lulls — FAA-H-8083-28B §10.7.2.
    • Turbulence — shear: vector wind change per 1,000 ft; ≥6 kt/1,000 ft = probable moderate-or-greater turbulence (FAA Aviation Weather Handbook). Thermal / mixing: daytime convective mixed layer below the boundary-layer top — FAA-H-8083-28B Ch.13 & USDA Agriculture Handbook 360, “Fire Weather” (the mixed layer commonly deepens to ~4,000–5,000 ft AGL by midafternoon; strong-wind mechanical mixing trends toward a dry-adiabatic lapse rate).
    • Inversion / mixing layer — diurnal cycle (nocturnal radiation inversion → daytime superadiabatic + adiabatic mixed layer) — FAA-H-8083-28B Ch.13 & Agriculture Handbook 360.
    • Icing — likely when temperature ≤0°C with visible moisture; clear 0 to −10°C, mixed −10 to −15°C, rime −15 to −20°C — NOAA/NWS Aviation Weather Center, Aviation Weather Guide: Icing (AviationWeather.gov).
    • Daylight & FAA night clocks — position lights sunset→sunrise (14 CFR §91.209(a)), anticollision lights whenever installed (§91.209(b)); “night” = end of evening to beginning of morning civil twilight (14 CFR §1.1); night passenger currency 1 h after sunset to 1 h before sunrise, same category & class, sole manipulator (14 CFR §61.57(b)). Solar geometry computed locally (sunrise/sunset at 90.833° zenith incl. refraction; civil twilight 96°).
    • Steering / drift — drift bearing = reciprocal of wind direction. Hodograph plots pressure-level winds (1000–700 hPa) by altitude.
    • Forecast confidence & best windows — NOAA/NCEP Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS, ~31 members) via the Open-Meteo Ensemble API; member agreement against your personal minimums.
    • Drift map & landing cone — single-forecast drift integrated from the wind profile; landing scatter from GEFS surface-wind member spread projected over the flight duration. Terrain — Copernicus GLO-90 (90 m) DEM via the Open-Meteo Elevation API (surface model — includes vegetation/buildings; 90 m smooths sharp peaks and won’t resolve individual towers). Great-circle distance — haversine, Earth radius 3,440.065 NM.
    Live data sources: Open-Meteo (forecast, ensemble, elevation) · NOAA/NWS api.weather.gov (backup) · RainViewer (radar) · Esri ArcGIS World Topo (map tiles) · OurAirports (airport database).
    Disclaimer. This is an educational planning aid. It is not an official weather briefing and is not a substitute for an FAA-approved briefing (Leidos Flight Service / 1-800-WX-BRIEF), AWC/NWS products, G-AIRMETs/SIGMETs, PIREPs, current METARs/TAFs, or a current sectional. The pilot in command is responsible for the final go/no-go decision.
